Mountain

The stage at FIAT sits in darkness before the lights find the first performer. The venue — converted from the automobile showroom its name remembers — holds its industrial DNA while serving entirely different purposes now. Tonight, theater.

"Mountain" arrives at FIAT as physical theater, dance, or something between categories. The production uses the body as primary vocabulary, the performers moving through narratives that language can't quite capture. The mountain of the title becomes metaphor — obstacle, aspiration, the thing that must be climbed or circumnavigated.

Physical theater requires different attention than text-based performance. The meaning lives in gesture, in the relationship between bodies in space, in the rhythm of movement and stillness. FIAT's industrial aesthetic provides the right container — no proscenium arch, no theater's usual signals. Just space and performers and whatever they build between.

The FIAT crowd has developed around programming that refuses easy categories. Visual artists, dancers, the Athens experimental scene that exists parallel to mainstream culture. You'll recognize them by how they watch — the specific attention that physical performance demands, the willingness to find meaning in forms that don't announce themselves.

The venue's history as automobile showroom creates unintentional resonance. The same floor that once displayed vehicles now hosts bodies in motion, the machinery replaced by something more fundamental. FIAT has reinvented itself as a space where Athens experimental culture gathers.

If you need narrative clarity and spoken dialogue, "Mountain" may frustrate you. Physical theater operates in registers that resist summary, creates meaning through accumulation rather than statement. But if you've been curious about what performance looks like when words step aside, when the body becomes the text — FIAT holds the ascent.

Ουρανός απ άλλους τόπους-ρόδα στο μαντίλι

The seats at Theatro Fournos are close enough to see the actors breathe. The space is intimate in the Greek theater tradition — no distant stages, no amplification creating distance between performer and witness. When "Ouranos ap' allous topous" begins, you're not watching. You're inside it.

The title translates to "Sky from Other Places" — and the production delivers on that promise of displacement. Greek theater has always grappled with questions of belonging and exile, of homes left behind and destinations never quite reached. This performance carries that tradition into contemporary territory, exploring what it means to look up at unfamiliar constellations.

Theatro Fournos occupies a specific position in Athens' theatrical landscape. The venue — its name means "Oven Theater" — has hosted experimental and traditional work since becoming one of the city's essential small stages. The space itself informs the work performed there, forcing intimacy, demanding that actors and audience share the same air.

The crowd for Greek-language theater at Fournos arrives with expectations. These are people who follow particular directors and playwrights, who read reviews in Athinorama and track what's happening beyond the mainstream houses. You'll find theater professionals alongside devoted audiences, people for whom a Thursday evening at Fournos represents the week's cultural anchor.

The performance unfolds with that particular intensity small-theater work allows. Every gesture visible, every whispered line audible, the space between performer and viewer collapsed to nothing. The subject matter — displacement, longing, the search for home under different skies — resonates differently in Athens, a city that has absorbed waves of arrival and departure across millennia.

If you need English supertitles, if Greek-language theater presents a barrier, this production asks for linguistic fluency. The intimacy works only if you can follow the words. But if you carry the language, if you've been looking for theater that treats its audience as intelligent participants, where the questions raised linger after the house lights come up — Theatro Fournos is exactly where this story should be told.
